title: docs: drop the roadmap and the dated dependency snapshot
description:
biohttp is flat, so `README.md` is the GitHub front page, the pkgdown home page
and the text CRAN renders. 215 lines down to 177.

## What was stale

| Line | Said | Now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Roadmap, row 5 | `done, 0.1.2 accepted 2026-09-03` | DESCRIPTION is 0.1.3 |
| Dependencies | `Resolved against CRAN on 2026-07-31`, four pinned versions | `pak::pkg_deps("biohttp")` |
| Dependencies | `The full recursive set is 14 non-base packages` | same |
| Citing | `Version 0.1.0 is 10.5281/zenodo.21731865` | `CITATION.cff`, which has all three |

The roadmap had six rows and every one said done. A table where nothing is
outstanding is a changelog, and `NEWS.md` already is one.

## Kept

The reasons `jsonlite`, `curl` and `tools` are declared. None of them is
guessable, and the `jsonlite` one in particular explains a failure that only
shows up at runtime on the package's main entry point.

The `Why` section stays. This is the page a CRAN reader lands on, and why the
package exists is the thing they are deciding.

## Moved

The compiled-code argument, including the 210ms against 0.2ms measurement, is
already in `CONTRIBUTING.md` in a longer form that names the alternatives. The
README keeps the conclusion and points there.

`CITATION.cff` needed no change. It already carries one identifier per archived
release, matching what Zenodo holds.

title: docs: drop the status note
description:
The note read:

> **Status:** on CRAN since 0.1.2. Docs at <https://www.samuelbharti.com/biohttp/>, and the current version is in `NEWS.md`. Every call returns the same shape, and that shape has not changed since 0.1.0. Changing it would be a breaking change.

It sends the reader to `NEWS.md` for the current version. `NEWS.md` leads with `# biohttp 0.1.3`, and `DESCRIPTION` agrees, but CRAN serves 0.1.2 and the newest tag is `v0.1.2`. So a reader who follows the pointer concludes 0.1.3 is released.

Everything else in it is stated better elsewhere:

- the version is on the badge row
- the return contract is the first bullet under `What it does`, which is more precise: "A call returns a value, never a condition. Transport failure, a non-success status code, and a 2xx with an unreadable body are three distinct outcomes the caller branches on."
- the stability promise is a versioning claim, which belongs in `NEWS.md`

The link to the documentation was kept as plain prose, because the note was the only place in the file it appeared.

title: docs: make the badge row honest and dependable
description:
The DOI badge came from `zenodo.org`, whose badge endpoints are not dependable. Measured over five requests each:

```
zenodo.org/badge/DOI/<doi>.svg     timed out x5, 15 seconds each
zenodo.org/badge/<repo-id>.svg     403 x5
img.shields.io/badge/DOI-...       200 x5, 0.08 to 0.16 seconds
```

That is why a DOI badge often fails to appear on first load and then shows up on a refresh. The browser gives up waiting, and a later cached fetch succeeds.

The replacement is served by shields and renders `DOI: 10.5281/zenodo....`:

```markdown
[![DOI](https://img.shields.io/badge/DOI-10.5281%2Fzenodo.21731864-1682D4)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21731864)
```

The slash becomes `%2F`, and `1682D4` is Zenodo's blue, so it still reads as a DOI badge.

It is also static, which fixes a second problem. `zenodo.org/badge/<repo-id>.svg` resolves to whatever Zenodo currently thinks is newest, while the link stays pinned to whatever was written, so after a release the image and the link can name different DOIs. With the DOI in both halves they cannot disagree.

## Lifecycle

Added, because every package should say what state it is in and none of them did. The stage follows CRAN: a package accepted there has users who can be broken by a change.

## Checked

The DOI resolves, and the badge renders, rather than being assumed.

title: chore: repair the shared history between main and dev
description:
Replaces #40, which could not merge.

## What was wrong

#37 was squash merged. That put `dev`'s content on `main` as one new commit
sharing no ancestry with the originals, so the merge base of `main` and `dev`
fell back to 1 August. Every change since then looked new on both sides, and
`DESCRIPTION`, `README.md` and `man/biohttp-package.Rd` conflicted, even though
the real difference is four files and +7 / -10.

It would have happened on every release, not just this one.

## The fix

This branch merges `dev` into `main` and resolves by taking `dev` everywhere.
The resulting tree hash is `231d5326`, identical to `dev`'s, so no content
changed. The merge exists for the ancestry.

Merge commits are enabled again. **Merge this one with a merge commit, not a
squash**, or the history breaks the same way. Squash stays on for feature
branches into `dev`.

## What ships

The docs site drops the Anthropic funder line (#39), `CITATION.cff` gains the
0.1.1 and 0.1.2 DOIs (#38), and the README acknowledgements section goes, since
pkgdown already prints those names from `DESCRIPTION`.

No code, no version change. Both branches stay on 0.1.3.

title: docs: correct the funder credit on the site
description:

Also here: the README acknowledgements section is gone, because pkgdown already

The commit list shows nine because #37 was squashed. The real change is four

```
CITATION.cff            the two new DOIs
DESCRIPTION             Anthropic removed
README.md               acknowledgements section removed
man/biohttp-package.Rd  regenerated
```

title: chore: correct who funded this
description:
## Anthropic was not a funder

`DESCRIPTION` listed Anthropic, PBC with the `fnd` role. What actually happened
is that part of a gifted Claude subscription was used while writing this. That
is a tool, in the same category as an IDE licence or a laptop, and it is not
money anyone put into the package.

`fnd` claims a relationship nobody agreed to. Removed from `DESCRIPTION` and
from the README.

It never reached CRAN. The published 0.1.2 is commit `de735df` from 23 August,
whose `Authors@R` lists the author alone; the funders arrived in #34, merged
today. The only place it went public is the documentation site, from the
deploy that followed #37 about an hour ago.

## Posit stays

They funded the early work during an internship. A funder credit is historical:
it does not stop being true when the funding ends, in the same way a package
keeps listing a grant after the grant closes.

Copyright is unchanged. Whether Posit holds copyright depends on the internship
agreement rather than on current funding, and that was confirmed separately
before this branch was written.

## The README acknowledgements section is gone

pkgdown builds a Developers list from `DESCRIPTION` and shows it in the home
page sidebar, so the live site was printing the same names twice on the same
page, a few pixels apart:

```
Developers
  Barret Schloerke        Thesis advisor
  Carson Sievert          Thesis advisor
  Posit Software, PBC     Copyright holder, funder
```

The generated version is the better one. It has precise role labels, it cannot
fall out of step with `DESCRIPTION`, and there is no tense to get wrong.

The prose copy is the one that had drifted. It still said Posit "funds it" in
the present tense, and it described the Anthropic subscription as a gift that
"supported the early stages and the planning of this work". Both were wrong,
and neither was wrong in `DESCRIPTION`, which is the argument for keeping one
copy rather than two.

Nothing is lost. The credit still appears in `?biohttp`, on the pkgdown authors
page, and in the home sidebar, and it will reach the CRAN page whenever 0.1.3
is submitted.

## Checks

440 tests, 0 lints, air and prek clean. No tracked file mentions Anthropic.

title: docs: list the 0.1.1 and 0.1.2 DOIs in CITATION.cff
description:
`CITATION.cff` has an `identifiers` list for people who want to pin the exact
version they used. It named only 0.1.0.

Two more have been archived since, and each DOI was minted after the file was
last edited, so nobody came back to add them:

| version | DOI | minted |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0.1.0 | `10.5281/zenodo.21731865` | 1 Aug |
| 0.1.1 | `10.5281/zenodo.21737380` | 1 Aug |
| 0.1.2 | `10.5281/zenodo.22635679` | 7 Sep, today |

Every one was checked against the Zenodo API before being written down, and
each resolves to the version it claims. A wrong number in a citation file is
the kind of thing nobody notices and everybody copies.

The concept DOI at the top of the file is unchanged. It is still the one to
cite, and it now resolves to 0.1.2, which is what CRAN serves.

Nothing else in the file moves, so the test asserting `DESCRIPTION`,
`.zenodo.json` and `CITATION.cff` agree on the version still passes.

title: release: 0.1.3
description:
Brings `main` up to date. It has been on 0.1.1 since 1 August, which is behind
both `dev` and CRAN.

Seven merges, 53 files, +1957 / -181.

## What is in it

**0.1.2, the version on CRAN.** #30 and #31. CRAN preparation: the disk cache
moved to `tools::R_user_dir()`, every environment variable now treats an empty
export the same as a missing one, and the Windows R-devel job joined CI. That
last one covers the combination CRAN's own incoming check runs, which nothing
here had been testing.

**0.1.3, not released anywhere yet.** #32 and #33. The batched path never
retried anything: `max_tries` was accepted by every batched entry point and did
nothing, because httr2 does not run its own retry policy under
`req_perform_parallel()`. Rate limits and `Retry-After` were read by no code
path in the batched direction. That is fixed, and `get_text_many()` plus a
per-call cache TTL came along with it.

**Housekeeping.** #34 credits advisors and funders. #35 got `dev` green after
#33 landed with two failing checks. #36 is a wording pass, and catches the
README up with being on CRAN.

## Worth knowing before this merges

`main` will read 0.1.3 while CRAN serves 0.1.2. That is deliberate. CRAN asks
for a month or two between updates without a serious reason, and 0.1.2 was
accepted four days ago, so 0.1.3 is not going to them yet.

This also publishes the docs site from `main`, so the site picks up the
rewritten README and reference pages.

## Checks

Every commit here was checked on its own PR. 440 tests, `R CMD check --as-cran`
0 errors 0 warnings, lintr and air clean.

title: fix: keep a sentence for a 2xx that turned out to be a failure
description:
Caught reviewing #26 before releasing, by diffing every status code against
0.1.0 rather than trusting the tests. Every test passed either way.

Routing `http_error_message()` through `classify_http()` made it return `NULL`
for a 2xx, because the enum correctly calls that `ok`. But this function''s
contract is a sentence, and a 2xx genuinely does reach it: a 200 carrying an
HTML error page, or a body that will not parse.

The envelope came out right regardless, because `status_error()` falls back when
its `error` is `NULL`, so it only bit a caller invoking the exported function
directly. Working by accident is still a defect.

| code | before this PR | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 200, 204 | `NULL` | `Could not retrieve data from S right now.` |
| everything else | unchanged | unchanged |

Now exactly one thing differs from 0.1.0, and it is a fix: a **408** says "took
too long to respond" instead of the generic message. `classify_http()` has
always called 408 a timeout, so the envelope said `timeout` while the sentence a
user read said something else. Documented in NEWS.

360 tests pass, check is 0 errors 0 warnings 2 known notes.

title: fix: redact the percent-encoded form of a query-string secret
description:
`redact_secrets()` matched only the raw secret value, but a secret reaches a URL
through `req_url_query()`, which percent-encodes it. A key holding `+`, `/` or
`=` survived redaction and landed in `res$detail`, which is the field an app
logs. Those are ordinary characters in a base64 key.

Before and after, same input:

```
secret        ab+cd/ef=gh
URL as sent   https://x.test/e?api_key=ab%2Bcd%2Fef%3Dgh
before        https://x.test/e?api_key=ab%2Bcd%2Fef%3Dgh   <- unchanged
after         https://x.test/e?api_key=<redacted>
```

The fix matches `curl::curl_escape()` as well as the raw value, because that is
the encoder httr2 builds query strings with, so the two cannot drift apart.

Every one of the twelve existing tests in `test-secrets.R` used an alphanumeric
secret (`SECRET123`, `abc123`, `ROTATED456`), which is exactly why nothing
caught this. Three tests added, including an end to end one that builds the
failure message from the URL the request actually carried.

`curl` is declared in Imports. It is already a hard dependency of httr2, so it
adds nothing to what a consumer installs, but the package now calls it directly
so it is named. The import guard test goes from four names to five, which is
the guard working as intended.

title: fix: add redact_secrets to the pkgdown reference index
description:
The pkgdown build on `dev` fails:

```
Error in `build_reference_index()`:
! In _pkgdown.yml, 1 topic missing from index: "redact_secrets".
```

`redact_secrets()` was exported in #5 without being added to the reference index, and pkgdown treats an unlisted exported topic as an error rather than a warning. It gets its own section rather than being tucked into an existing one, because it is the entry point for a rule callers need to read: which credentials belong in the query string and which belong in a header.

Verified with `pkgdown::build_reference_index()`, which now completes.

title: feat: let a caller supply its own user-facing error strings
description:
Set `biohttp.status_message` to a function of `source`, `status`, `http` and
`condition` and it replaces the built-in wording. That is what lets an app keep
its own voice, or localise, while adopting the transport.

Returning anything other than a single non-empty string falls back to the
built-in, so covering one status and leaving the rest is the expected way to use
it rather than a mistake.

**The override runs inside `tryCatch()`.** It sits on the failure path, which is
exactly where the package promises never to raise, and someone else's bug must
not be able to break that. There is a test for it.

**The scope was wider than the issue described.** The strings lived in two
places, and they had already drifted three ways for the same condition:

| Source | String |
| --- | --- |
| `status_error()` default | `X is temporarily unavailable.` |
| `http_error_message()` 5xx | `...unavailable. Please try again.` |
| `http_error_message()` fallback | `...unavailable. Please try again shortly.` |

`status_no_data()`, `status_rate_limited()` and `status_timeout()` each held a
duplicate of a sentence that also lived in `http_error_message()`. A hook on
`http_error_message()` alone would have left all of those unreachable. They now
route through one function, with a test asserting a constructor and the message
function cannot disagree.

**One user-visible change:** `status_error()`'s default gains "Please try
again.", matching the other two.

`graphql_error()` keeps its own distinct sentence. A GraphQL query error is a
body-content outcome rather than one of the seven transport statuses, so it does
not fit the override signature; worth a follow-up if you want it covered.

334 tests pass, check is 0 errors 0 warnings 2 known notes, and the pkgdown
reference index has the new export so the site still builds.

Closes #23

title: fix: keep a held cache reference valid across a reset
description:
Stacked on #24, which adds `BIOHTTP_CACHE_MAX_N`, because the config comparison
has to know about it.

`cache_reset()` set the store to `NULL`, so the next `cache()` built a new
object and any reference taken earlier kept pointing at the orphan. Silent in
both directions: writes went where nothing else could see them, reads returned
stale entries.

**Neither option in the issue works as written.** Resetting in place
unconditionally is the obvious fix, and it breaks the package's own tests:
`test-cache.R` toggles `BIOHTTP_CACHE_DISK` and asserts the store class flips
between `cache_mem` and `cache_layered`, which never happens if the object is
only ever cleared. The reporter suspected the rebuild might be deliberate. It
is, and the suite depends on it.

So the reset is config-aware. Settings unchanged, clear in place and the held
reference stays valid. Settings changed, drop and rebuild as before.

The issue's repro, now:

```
held$size()           0
live$size()           0
identical(held, live) TRUE
live$exists('k2')     TRUE
```

Every line is inverted from the report except the sizes, which are 0 because
the reset did its job.

**Residual gap, documented rather than engineered around.** A reference held
across a genuine settings change is still orphaned. Nothing changes cache
settings mid-run except a test suite, and tests do not hold references.

Closes #21

title: feat: add the hex logo
description:
Wires `man/figures/logo.png` and `logo.svg` into the README and the site.
pkgdown prefers the SVG for the navbar and generates the favicon set from it,
so the site now has proper icons for the first time.

**The theme needed retuning.** `_pkgdown.yml` still carried `primary: #1a6b54`,

green links directly beside a rust hex. It is now `#8a3a30`, taken from the
logo. The darker rust rather than the orange, because `primary` drives link text
and `#d98346` does not have the contrast for that on a light background.

Verified on a local build: the logo is referenced in `index.html`, all five
favicon links are present, and the built Bootstrap CSS carries the new colour 30
times with no trace of the old green.

Also documents installing from GitHub with `pak` or `remotes`, for anyone who
needs an unreleased commit rather than the r-universe build.

314 tests pass, `R CMD check --as-cran` is 0 errors 0 warnings 2 known notes.

One upstream nit, not introduced here and not worth working around: pkgdown
emits the SVG favicon link with curly quotes in the `type` attribute, so
browsers ignore that one and fall back to the `.ico` and `.png`. Icons still
work everywhere.

title: feat: carry query-string credentials safely
description:
Stacked on #4. Retarget to `dev` once that merges; GitHub will do it automatically.

Adds `secret_query` to `get_json()`, `post_json()`, `get_text()`, `perform()`, `perform_text()`, and the batched wrappers, plus an exported `redact_secrets()`.

## Why this exists

NCBI E-utilities raises a caller from 3 to 10 requests a second with an `api_key` parameter, and offers no header form. The credential has to travel in the URL.

That is a different problem from a header credential in three ways, and all three are handled:

1. **It would land in the cache key**, which is built from the URL. Adding or rotating a key would silently invalidate every entry the process had already cached.
2. **It would print.** `print(req)`, an inspected request, or a traceback all show `req$url` verbatim.
3. **It would reach an error message.** A transport failure carries the curl message, which usually contains the URL that failed.

The fix for the first two is to keep the credential out of the request object entirely and attach it only at dispatch, inside `perform_with()`. The request a caller holds, and the URL the cache key is built from, never contain it. The fix for the third is `redact_secrets()`, applied to every message built from a condition.

## httr2 has no redaction for query parameters

`req_url_query()` accepts a `.redact` argument without erroring and treats it as another query parameter. Passing one produces:

```
...esearch.fcgi?db=clinvar&api_key=SECRET123&.redact=api_key
```

The secret stays in the clear and the attempt to redact it is advertised. This package therefore does the redaction itself rather than delegating it.

## What this is not for

`secret_query` is deliberately excluded from the cache key, so two calls differing only in their credential are treated as the same call. That suits a credential that changes a rate limit or a quota. A credential that changes *what comes back* must go in `headers`, which is part of the key. `SECURITY.md` states the rule.

A query-string credential still reaches the server's access logs. That is a property of the service, not something a client can fix, and the docs say so.

## Verification

`R CMD check`: Status OK, zero notes. 18 new tests, including one asserting that the same call with no key, with a key, and with a rotated key makes exactly one request.

title: feat: batch requests to one host at a time
description:
Adds `perform_many()`, `get_json_many()`, and `post_json_many()`, plus the 0.1.0 and 0.2.0 release commits that had not reached `dev`.

## What this is for

Many questions to ONE source. A gene list or a variant list is nearly always that shape, and asking one at a time spends the round trip over and over on a call that is already almost entirely waiting.

Results come back the same length and in the same order as the input, so a caller zips them back on by position. Cache keys are built exactly the way the single-call wrappers build theirs, so a batch reuses entries a single call warmed and the other way around. A failed entry is still never cached.

## Same host, not a mix

httr2 documents `req_perform_parallel()` as applying `req_throttle()` and `req_retry()` across the whole list rather than per request, and says plainly that it is "most suitable for performing many parallel requests to the same host, rather than a mix of different hosts". A throttled request to one host would make an unthrottled request to another wait behind it.

So this batches within a host and groups by host to keep that true even when a caller passes a mixed list. Host groups run one after another.

This contradicts what the original plan assumed. Cross-service fan-out needs process-level concurrency with a daemon pool that has a lifecycle, and that belongs in an application rather than here.

## The breaker

httr2's own circuit breaker never fires under parallel performance, which is part of why this package carries its own. A host with an open breaker is never dispatched to and every one of its requests comes back `skipped`. Once a batch is in flight a failure cannot short-circuit the rest, so transport failures within a batch take effect on the next call rather than the current one.

## Verification

`R CMD check`: Status OK, zero notes. `classify_result()` is shared between the serial and batched paths, with a test asserting the signature so the two cannot drift apart -- two copies of the failure classification is how the four app-local layers diverged in the first place.

title: feat: freeze the envelope contract and release 0.1.0
description:
Phase 2 of the foundation plan. Freezes the envelope contract, ships the
migration shim, writes the vignette, and tags 0.1.0.

> **Stacked on #2**, which is stacked on #1. Merge those first and this shrinks
> to its own three commits.

## The contract is public from here

Section 4.5 settled Shape B, and the transport in #2 already returns it. This
release makes that a commitment: after 0.1.0, changing the envelope is a
breaking change.

`vignette("biohttp")` is the deliverable. It documents the one rule (a call
returns a value, it never raises), the eight fields, the seven statuses, the
`error` and `detail` split, how to build a client, credentials, throttling, the
breaker rule, the cache rules, GraphQL, and how to test a client.

It also documents the trap I hit in #2: `httr2::with_mocked_responses()` sits
below the retry loop, so a mocked 503 arrives exactly once regardless of
`max_tries`. Anyone testing retry needs a real server.

## `as_legacy_envelope()`

Deprecated on arrival, removal scheduled for 0.3.0. It exists so
`variant-reviewer` and `genescout` can adopt biohttp without rewriting every
call site in the same PR.

It warns once per session rather than once per call, because a migration runs it
in a loop and a warning per request would bury the signal.

The tests spell out what the old shape loses: `skipped` flattens into an
ordinary failure, and there is no way to reconstruct it afterwards. That is the
argument for migrating off the shim rather than settling on it.

## Also in here

`Suggests` gains `knitr` and `rmarkdown` for the vignette. `Imports` is
unchanged at four, and the guard test still enforces it.

## Verification

All local, since the Actions quota is out.

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `R CMD check --as-cran` | 0 errors, 0 warnings, 2 notes |
| `devtools::test()` | 264 pass, 0 fail |
| `air format --check .` | clean |
| `lintr::lint_package()` | no lints |
| `prek run --all-files` | 11 hooks pass |
| `pkgdown::build_site()` | builds, vignette included |

The vignette is built by `R CMD check`, so it is executed rather than just
rendered. Both remaining notes are the ones from #2: the private repo's 404 URLs,
which clear at Phase 3, and a stray `'NULL'` directory that this Windows R
install creates for any package with an example.

## Next

Phase 3 publishes to r-universe, which needs the repo public. Phase 4 migrates
`variant-reviewer` and proves the Docker bundle still restores.

title: feat: port the transport layer from multi-variant-reviewer
description:
Phase 1 of the foundation plan. Ports the transport layer out of
`multi-variant-reviewer` so the four hand-copied HTTP layers can start
collapsing into one installed package.

> **Stacked on #1.** This branch is cut from `feat/scaffold`, because Phase 0 has
> not merged yet. Until it does, the diff below includes #1's four commits. Merge
> #1 first and this shrinks to the four transport commits, or merge this one and
> it carries both.

## What lands

`R/envelope.R`, `R/breaker.R`, `R/request.R`, `R/errors.R`, `R/perform.R`,
`R/cache.R`, `R/utils.R`. 1243 lines of R, 743 of tests, 230 tests passing.

Ported from `multi-variant-reviewer/R/{http,status,cache}.R`, which the scoping
report names as the superset. `genescout`'s text handling comes across as
`perform_text()` and `get_text()`, returning the body in `data` rather than a
separate `text` field, so there is one envelope shape rather than two.

The disk cache tier is opt-in and off by default, per section 6 rule 2. A
library should not start writing to somebody's disk because they installed it.

## Three things worth reviewing closely

**The plan's note about `knowledge-graph-viewer` was backwards.** It said KG and
MVR treat an unreadable body the same way. They do the opposite. KG calls
`.kg_breaker_record(host, ok = FALSE)` when the parse fails, so a garbage body
counts against the host, and its comment says that is deliberate. `genescout` and
`variant-reviewer` land in the same place accidentally, by wrapping perform and
parse in one `tryCatch` and reading `is.na(status)` as unreachable. MVR is the
only one of the four that records the host reachable before parsing.

MVR's behaviour is what the plan mandates in its own sections 3.1 and 6, and MVR
is the declared source of truth, so that is what shipped. Each of the three
failure classes now has its own named breaker assertion in `test-perform.R`.

**`cachem::cache_disk()` does not error on a directory it cannot use.** It warns
and hands back a normal-looking object, and the failure surfaces later on a real
`set()`, mid-call. So the `tryCatch(..., error = )` inherited from MVR never
fired and the documented memory-only fallback did not happen. `disk_tier()` now
constructs, writes a probe entry, reads it back, and only then layers the tier.
Tested with a path under a regular file, which fails `dir.create()` everywhere.

**`jsonlite` had to go into Imports.** httr2 keeps it in Suggests, and
`resp_body_json()` calls `check_installed("jsonlite")` at runtime, so with three
imports the package installs cleanly and then fails on the first `get_json()`.
It costs nothing real: `shiny` imports `jsonlite` directly, so every consumer app
already has it.

Also: cachem keys allow lowercase letters and numbers only, not the
`^[a-z0-9._-]+$` the original comment claimed. `rlang::hash()` was never at risk,
but the test now pins the real rule.

## Open question for review

The plan names bare functions but never named the envelope constructors. MVR has
`mvr_ok`, `mvr_err`, `mvr_skipped`; dropping the prefix gives `ok()`,
`timeout()`, `stale()`, too generic to export. This uses `status_ok()`,
`status_no_data()`, `status_stale()`, `status_rate_limited()`,
`status_timeout()`, `status_skipped()`, `status_error()`. Cheap to rename now,
painful once Phase 2 freezes the contract and `bioclients` builds on it.

## Verification

All local, since the Actions quota is out.

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `R CMD check --as-cran` | 0 errors, 0 warnings, 2 notes |
| `devtools::test()` | 230 pass, 0 fail |
| `air format --check .` | clean |
| `lintr::lint_package()` | no lints |
| `prek run --all-files` | 11 hooks pass |
| `pkgdown::build_site()` | builds |

Both notes are benign and were checked rather than assumed. "CRAN incoming
feasibility" is the private repo returning 404 to anonymous fetches, which clears
at Phase 3. "Non-standard things in the check directory" reports a stray `'NULL'`
directory that this Windows R 4.6.1 install creates for any package with an
example: a throwaway package with one function and a single `add_one(1)` example
reproduces it exactly.

Tests are offline. No test hits a real host.

title: feat: scaffold the biohttp package
description:
Phase 0 of the foundation plan. Scaffolds the package so Phase 1 can port the
transport into a working harness rather than a blank directory. No transport
code lands here.

## What is in it

- Package skeleton: DESCRIPTION, MIT license, roxygen, NEWS, testthat harness.
- `Imports` is `httr2`, `cachem`, and `rlang`, and nothing else. Two tests
  assert that, and that no Shiny dependency appears in any field. The
  dependency list is a hard constraint rather than a preference, since every
  downstream app inherits it, so a change to it should fail the suite and force
  the conversation.
- Tooling adapted from `biobouncer`: air, lintr, prek hooks, gitattributes.
- Governance: code of conduct, contributing, security policy, citation file.
- CI: R CMD check on five platforms, lintr, prek, gitleaks, conventional PR
  titles, and a pkgdown build.

## Two things worth a look

`_pkgdown.yml` sets `destination: _site`. pkgdown defaults to writing into
`docs/`, which is where the working plans live, so the two collide. The site
gets its own directory instead.

`.Rbuildignore` has nine more entries than `biobouncer`'s copy. In that repo the
`pkg-r/` subdirectory hid the tooling from `R CMD build` for free. Here the
package root is the repo root, so each tooling file has to be named or it turns
into a check note.

## Verification

Run locally, since the Actions quota is out:

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `R CMD check --as-cran` | 0 errors, 0 warnings, 1 note |
| `air format --check .` | clean |
| `lintr::lint_package()` | no lints |
| `prek run --all-files` | 11 hooks pass |
| `pkgdown::build_site()` | builds |

The remaining note is `checking CRAN incoming feasibility`. It reports "New
submission", the development version number, and four URLs returning 404. The
404s are the GitHub and pkgdown URLs, which are not reachable anonymously while
the repo is private. That clears itself at Phase 3.

Expect the CI checks on this PR to fail to start. That is the exhausted Actions
quota, not the code.

title: feat: bound the cache by entry count as well as age and size
description:
`max_size` bounds bytes, not entries. A long-running process answering many
small responses stays well under it while holding far more entries than
intended, which is exactly the case the reporter hit moving an app that had
`max_n = 5000`.

`BIOHTTP_CACHE_MAX_N` is now passed to `cache_mem(max_n = )`, defaulting to
cachem's own `Inf` so nothing changes unless it is set.

Proven the test is meaningful rather than vacuous:

```
without max_n (0.1.0 behaviour):  3 entries
with max_n = 2:                   2 entries
oldest evicted under lru:         TRUE
```

**One correction to the issue.** It suggests also setting `evict = "lru"`
explicitly, on the basis that it is currently an inherited default. It is not.
`R/cache.R` has set it since the original transport port, and it is in the
`v0.1.0` tag. The `deparse()` output quoted in the issue omits it, so that was
read from something other than shipped 0.1.0.

Also documents `BIOHTTP_CACHE_MAX_SIZE` and `BIOHTTP_CACHE_DISK_TTL`, which the
vignette table had never listed.

Closes #22

title: docs: say the package is on r-universe, because it now is
description:
The status line said "not on r-universe yet" while the install section,
rewritten alongside the logo, described installing from it. `dev` both denied
and assumed the same fact. Both statements are now true.

biohttp 0.1.0 is built on r-universe with binaries for R 4.5.3, 4.6.0, 4.6.1
and 4.7.0.

Verified rather than assumed. Installed from r-universe into a clean library,
loaded it, and made a call:

```
installed: TRUE
version:   0.1.0
call works: TRUE - ok - BRCA1
```

Adds the r-universe version badge and marks phase 3 of the roadmap done.

title: ci: check every pull request, not only those into main
description:
The workflows were limited to pull requests into `main` because Actions minutes
were exhausted. The repository is public now and standard runners are free, so
that trade only costs safety.

Every pull request runs the full set again, into `dev` as well as `main`.
Pushes stay off: a branch is checked when it is proposed, and the same commits
do not need checking twice. The push to `main` still publishes the site.

`secret-scan` is the one that mattered most. A credential could reach `dev` with
no server-side scan at all, and the local gitleaks hook only helps someone who
installed the hooks.

CONTRIBUTING is updated to match, since it described the restricted arrangement.

This pull request is its own proof: it targets `dev`, so if the checks run here
the change works.

title: docs: add the Zenodo DOI
description:
The release is archived: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21731864

Zenodo minted two DOIs, and the distinction matters for what goes in a badge.
The concept DOI (`...864`) always resolves to the newest release. The version
DOI (`...865`) is fixed to 0.1.0. The badge and the suggested citation use the
concept DOI, and `CITATION.cff` records the version DOI under `identifiers` for
anyone who needs to pin what they actually used.

Also adds a short "Citing biohttp" section to the README.

Verified the archived record: title, version 0.1.0, creator with ORCID, and
license all came through correctly. The license reads `mit-license`, so the
`"license": "mit"` value in `.zenodo.json` was accepted rather than falling back
to the repository license.

All three URLs return 200. 314 tests pass, check is 0 errors 0 warnings 2 known
notes, prek clean.

title: docs: make the package read as a standalone project
description:
Preparing the repository to be public.

The README named three private repositories, listed their internal file paths
(`R/http.R`, `R/api_http.R`, `R/cache.R`), and described their known defects
("the copies have drifted", "a latent `.Rprofile` bug was fixed in some but not
all", "raises instead of returning"). Source comments, the migration shim docs,
and the `user_agent()` examples named them too, and `.gitignore` named a private
planning repo.

None of that is needed to explain what the package does, and together it
disclosed the existence, layout, and weaknesses of repositories that are not
public.

The "Why" section now states the general problem instead of describing a
specific family of apps. Named references become generic: "a client package
built on top", "an application that already returns the older four-field shape",
"one daemon per host, through something like mirai". The `user_agent()` examples
use `my-shiny-app` and `my-client-package`.

Also dropped "a transitive dependency of six Shiny apps and a Docker image",
which discloses a fleet size and means nothing to an outside reader.

A regex sweep for every removed term comes back clean across the tree.

title: feat: collapse repeated queries within one batch
description:
Three queries where two are identical sent three requests. Verified before the
change: 3 queries in, 3 requests out.

The cache cannot collapse them on its own. Everything in a batch is in flight at
once, so the duplicate is dispatched long before the original has an entry to
serve. Deduplication has to happen before dispatch.

`cached_many()` now sends one request per distinct cache key and hands the
result back to every position that asked for it, so the returned list is still
the same length and order as the input.

Two tests. The first pins the request count and that both positions get the
answer. The second pins that fanning one result out to several positions did
not become a back door around the success-only cache rule: a repeated failing
query is still not stored.

title: ci: limit workflows to the release gate and publish the docs site
description:
Three things, all about where checks run and what they produce.

**Workflows only run at the release gate.** Every workflow ran on pushes to
`dev` and on pull requests into any branch, so routine feature work spent
Actions minutes on checks that already run locally. All five are now limited to
`main`: a pull request into it, and the push when it merges.

**gitleaks moved local.** Secret scanning only ran in CI, so a credential was
caught after it had already been committed and pushed. It now runs as a prek
hook on every commit. Verified against a planted token: a GitHub PAT is caught
and AWS documentation example keys are correctly allowlisted.

**The docs site now publishes.** The pkgdown job built the site and threw the
artifact away. A deploy job publishes to Pages, gated on a push to `main`. A
pull request still stops after the build, which proves the site builds without
publishing anything.

Also folds in the two pkgdown build fixes from #6, which this supersedes:
`redact_secrets` was missing from the reference index, and
`build_site_github_pages()` defaults `dest_dir` to `docs/`, overriding the
destination in `_pkgdown.yml`, so the site was written where the upload step
was not looking.

CONTRIBUTING and SECURITY are updated to describe what actually runs where.

Verified locally: 314 tests pass, `R CMD check --as-cran` 0 errors 0 warnings
2 known notes, 0 lints, air clean, prek clean.

title: chore: release 0.1.1
description:
Version bump for #21, #22 and #23.

Moves `DESCRIPTION`, `.zenodo.json` and `CITATION.cff` together, with a
`NEWS.md` section covering the three.

**Adds a guard so this cannot drift again.** The version lives in three files
and nothing read it from one source. `.zenodo.json` is what a release is
archived under and `CITATION.cff` is what GitHub renders in the cite box, so
either going stale mislabels the record permanently, in a way nobody notices
until someone cites it.

Proven the guard actually fires rather than being vacuous:

```
FAILURE: 'test-package.R:49:3'
`actual`: "9.9.9"
[ FAIL 1 | WARN 0 | SKIP 0 | PASS 4 ]
```

347 tests pass, check is 0 errors 0 warnings 2 known notes.

title: chore: prepare the repository to be public
description:
Batched so it costs one CI run rather than several.

**README status line.** It said "Not published yet" while the documentation
site is live. Now names r-universe specifically and links the site.

**Zenodo metadata.** Adds `.zenodo.json` so the archived release carries
deliberate title, description, ORCID, license, and keywords rather than
whatever Zenodo infers from the repository. `CITATION.cff` gains
`date-released`, which a citation needs and Zenodo reads. Both are in
`.Rbuildignore`, so the check output is unchanged.

**Code of conduct.** It said reports go "to the maintainer" without saying how.
Now gives an address and states that a reporter's identity is kept
confidential.

**Issue and pull request templates.** A first-time contributor gets told the
scope rules and the local check commands before spending effort rather than
after. The bug template asks for an offline reproducible example, since a
report that depends on a live host cannot be acted on later.

Verified locally: 314 tests pass, `R CMD check --as-cran` 0 errors 0 warnings
2 known notes, prek clean, and both metadata files parse.

title: chore: reset the version to 0.1.0
description:
`DESCRIPTION` said 0.3.0. There were three `chore: release` commits, zero git
tags, a private repo, and nothing published. Three releases declared, none of
which existed.

Bumping the minor twice before anything shipped invents a history that did not
happen and burns two version numbers on work no consumer has seen. This is all
one unreleased first version.

It also fixes a contradiction that had appeared: `as_legacy_envelope()` was
exported at 0.3.0 while its own docs and runtime warning said it was scheduled
for removal *in 0.3.0*. It named the version it would vanish in and then shipped
in it. At 0.1.0 that target is two releases out and coherent again.

`NEWS.md` collapses to a single 0.1.0 section covering the transport, batching,
and query-string credentials together. `CITATION.cff` still said `0.0.0.9000`,
which is the version GitHub renders in the cite box, so it is corrected too.

Tag `v0.1.0` when it actually ships.

title: docs: say things plainly and catch up with CRAN
description:
A wording pass over the documentation, plus catching the README up with the
fact that we are on CRAN now. No behaviour changes.

## Stop sending people away

`get_json_many()`, `get_text_many()` and `post_json_many()` all opened with:

> Read the sections on `perform_many()` first. The same two rules apply: pass
> requests for one host, and supply a `throttle`.

If you open `?get_json_many` you get told to go read something else before you
are told what the function does. The two rules are one sentence, so they are
just said:

> Send requests for one host, and pass a `throttle`. `perform_many()` explains
> both.

## The README did not know we were on CRAN

0.1.2 has been on CRAN since 3 September, and the README still said to install
from r-universe. The badge and the `install.packages()` line were held back
deliberately in #30, because both point at a URL that 404s until acceptance and
the README ships inside the tarball. That reason has expired.

* CRAN badge added.
* Installation opens with `install.packages("biohttp")`. r-universe and GitHub
  stay below it.
* The roadmap said "CRAN submission | in progress". It says done.

**A real bug while in there.** The README told people to run:

```r
pak::pak("samuelbharti/biohttp@v0.1.2")
```

There is no `v0.1.2` tag. Only `v0.1.0` and `v0.1.1` exist, because 0.1.2 went
to CRAN without ever being tagged. That command fails for anyone who copies it.
It now points at `v0.1.1` and links the releases page so the example does not
rot the same way again. The real fix is tagging 0.1.2, which is a separate
decision.

## "Envelope contract"

Gone from the front page. It asked the reader to accept a term before seeing a
single example. "Every call returns the same shape, and that shape has not
changed since 0.1.0" says the same thing and needs nothing explained first.
Same edit in the roadmap.

## Titles that read like implementation notes

| before | after |
| --- | --- |
| Classify an HTTP status code onto the status enum | Turn an HTTP status code into a status |
| Classify a transport condition onto the status enum | Turn a failed connection into a status |
| Build an attributable User-Agent string | Build a User-Agent that identifies your caller |
| Per-host transport dispatch counts | How many requests went out, per host |
| Clear all transport dispatch counters | Clear the request counts |

## The jsonlite note

`?biohttp` carried a section explaining why jsonlite is imported but never
called. It is good reasoning aimed at the wrong reader: it is a packaging
decision, not something a user needs on screen. It is a comment in
`R/biohttp-package.R` now, where the next maintainer will find it.

## Vignette

"Writing a client **with** biohttp" rather than "against". Against read like
you were fighting it.

## Checks

440 tests, 0 lints, `R CMD check --as-cran` 0 errors 0 warnings, air and prek
clean, pkgdown builds. 49 lines added, 51 removed.

title: chore: acknowledge advisors and funders across the package
description:
Adds the same author and acknowledgement metadata that biobouncer carries:
two thesis advisors, Posit Software, PBC as a funder and copyright holder,
and the early support from Anthropic.

## What changes

* `Authors@R` gains Barret Schloerke and Carson Sievert as thesis advisors
  (`ths`) and Posit Software, PBC as copyright holder and funder (`cph`,
  `fnd`), plus Anthropic as a funder (`fnd`). Copyright holders are
  unchanged from what the LICENSE files already say: Samuel Bharti and
  Posit Software, PBC.
* `LICENSE` and `LICENSE.md` list both copyright holders.
* `_pkgdown.yml` lists the advisors and funders on the docs home page
  sidebar (`roles: [aut, cre, ths, fnd]`). The footer keeps the pkgdown
  default, which now reads the added roles automatically.
* `README.md` gains a short Acknowledgements section, next to the existing
  Citing section.
* `man/biohttp-package.Rd` is regenerated by roxygen2.

`CITATION.cff`, `.zenodo.json`, and `inst/CITATION` are left as is, matching
the choice made in biobouncer to keep citation authorship to the maintainer.

## Checks

* `roxygen2::roxygenise(".")` regenerates cleanly.
* `prek run --all-files` passes.

title: feat: batched text downloads and a per call cache ttl
description:
## What

Two additions to the transport layer, one per commit.

1. `get_text_many()`, the batched counterpart to `get_text()`. It wires the
   existing `perform_many_with()` and `read_text_body()` together, so the
   breaker rule and the three failure classes come from the same code path as
   every other entry point. Cache keys are built exactly as `get_text()` builds
   them (`GET_TEXT <url>` plus headers), so a batch reuses a file a single call
   fetched and the other way around.

2. A `ttl` argument (seconds, `NULL` for the configured default) on
   `get_json()`, `post_json()`, `get_text()`, and the three `_many()` wrappers,
   passed through `cached()` and `cached_many()`. The case is a bulk table that
   should outlive the 1800 s `BIOHTTP_CACHE_TTL` default without raising it for
   every one-record lookup.

## How the ttl works

cachem 1.1.0 has no per-entry age: `set()` takes a key and a value, and
`max_age` is one number for the whole store. So the memory tier is now built
with `max_age = Inf` and each stored value carries its own `expires_at`.
`cache_get()` treats an entry past its time as a miss and removes it. A value
written straight through `cache()$set()` has no expiry and passes through
unchanged. The disk tier keeps `BIOHTTP_CACHE_DISK_TTL` as a hard ceiling.

One consequence worth knowing: an expired entry now sits in memory until it is
read or evicted by `BIOHTTP_CACHE_MAX_SIZE` / `BIOHTTP_CACHE_MAX_N`, where
before cachem pruned it by age on the next write. Both ceilings still bound the
store.

`BIOHTTP_CACHE_TTL` moved out of `cache_config()` because the store no longer
depends on it at build time; it is read at each write instead.

## Tests

- webfakes server with two text endpoints (TSV and CSV) read through
  `get_text_many()` over a real socket.
- `get_text()` and `get_text_many()` share entries both ways, and the text
  keyspace stays separate from the JSON one for the same URL.
- A long ttl survives a short `BIOHTTP_CACHE_TTL`; a short ttl expires; the
  configured default applies when none is passed; an expired entry is removed
  on read; ttl is validated on every entry point; the batched path honors it.
  The clock is mocked with `local_mocked_bindings(cache_now = ...)` rather
  than slept through.

## Docs

The vignette's cache section gains one paragraph on per-call lifetime, and the
`BIOHTTP_CACHE_TTL` table row now reads "default lifetime of an entry". README
and pkgdown reference list `get_text_many()`. No version bump.

title: fix: get dev green again
description:
`dev` has been red since 31 August. #33 went in with two failing checks and
nothing stopped it, because `dev` is not branch protected. CI only runs on pull
requests, so a broken `dev` stays quiet until the next PR picks it up. That is
what #34 has been showing.

Both failures came from #33. Neither is big.

## The lint

`tests/testthat/test-parallel-retry.R:135` used `<<-`:

```r
seen <<- c(seen, path)
```

It now writes to an environment, the same way `tries <- new.env()` two lines
above already does.

Worth knowing why this got through. CI installs `any::lintr` and picked up
**3.4.0**. Our local install was **3.3.0.1**, which reports zero lints on the
broken tree. So a local check said clean and was simply blind to it. I have
upgraded the local copy, and checked the fix against the version CI uses:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 3.4.0 on the file as it is on `dev` | 1 lint, line 135 |
| 3.4.0 on the fixed file | 0 |

The suite has 30 uses of `<<-` and 3.4.0 flags only this one, including seven
others in the same file. So this really is one line, not a suite-wide cleanup.
I left the rest alone.

## The pkgdown index

#33 exported five functions and did not add them to `_pkgdown.yml`, so
`build_reference_index()` stops:

```
! In _pkgdown.yml, 5 topics missing from index: "ratelimit_record", ...
```

They go in two new sections rather than being appended somewhere convenient:

* **Rate limiting**: `ratelimit_record`, `ratelimit_wait`, `ratelimit_reset`.
  These sit next to the circuit breaker, since both hold per-host state.
* **What the transport did**: `transport_stats`, `transport_stats_reset`.
  These follow the cache.

The index now covers every topic exactly once: 37 Rd files, 37 entries, no
gaps, nothing listed twice, nothing pointing at a topic that does not exist.

## Checks

* `pkgdown::build_site()` builds, which is the real reproduction of the failing
  job
* 406 tests pass
* `R CMD check --as-cran`: 0 errors, 0 warnings
* `air format --check`, `prek run --all-files`: clean

## What this does not do

`dev` is still unprotected, so the same thing can happen again. Worth fixing
separately.

title: feat(parallel): retry rate-limited and transient failures in the batched path
description:
The batched path (post_json_many() and friends, via req_perform_parallel()) never retried anything: max_tries was accepted and silently ignored, Retry-After was never read, and a rate-limited host got hit again at the same rate that just triggered the limit. Confirmed against a local always-429 webfakes server: 6 requests, 6 hits, 70ms, zero retries.

Root cause: req_defaults() disarms httr2's req_error() so perform() can classify a non-2xx instead of catching a condition. That is correct and stays, but it also means httr2's own transient-retry machinery (which reads Retry-After) never engages under req_perform_parallel(). This PR adds biohttp's own capped retry over failed indices instead of re-arming req_error (httr2 1.2.3's queue-level can_retry() is unconditionally TRUE, so re-arming would risk unbounded retries).

## What changed

- perform_many_with() now retries: a pass after the first re-sends only requests that came back rate_limited, timeout, or a 5xx. A settled answer (ok, no_data, any other 4xx) is never retried. max_tries, already accepted by every batched entry point, now actually does something.
- New ratelimit.R: a per-host pause ledger, separate from the circuit breaker. Set from a 429/503's Retry-After (httr2::resp_retry_after()) or an exponential-backoff fallback, honored before the next dispatch to that host.
- New stats.R: transport_stats() / transport_stats_reset(), per-host dispatched/retried/rate_limited counts, for a caller to verify what a run actually did instead of guessing from wall-clock time.
- envelope() and status_rate_limited() gain a retry_after field.
- The breaker's rule is unchanged: a 429 still proves the host is reachable and clears its failure count (breaker.R is about transport reachability, not rate limiting). Pacing a rate-limited host is the new ledger's job.
- max_tries on get_json_many()/post_json_many() now retries by default (3). A caller relying on the old silent single-dispatch behavior should pass max_tries = 1 explicitly; four pre-existing cache/dedupe tests were updated this way since they test caching, not retry.

## Local checks

Full suite: 406 pass, 0 fail. lintr: 0 lints. prek: clean. Version bumped to 0.1.3 (DESCRIPTION, .zenodo.json, CITATION.cff kept in sync per the package's own version-agreement test); NEWS.md entry added.

title: chore: prepare the package for a CRAN submission
description:
## What this changes

Makes the package submittable to CRAN, and releases 0.1.2 to carry it.

The prompt for this was CRAN's review of a sibling package, biobouncer. Checking
its three comments against biohttp:

| CRAN comment on biobouncer | Applies here? |
| --- | --- |
| Add method references to the description as `authors (year) <doi:...>` | Conditional, and now pre-empted. The breaker is Nygard's Circuit Breaker pattern, cited as `Nygard (2018, ISBN:9781680502398)`. |
| Never comment out code in examples | **No.** All 31 example blocks execute. The five comment lines inside examples are explanatory prose, not disabled code. Checked line by line. |
| Wrap examples needing `Suggests` packages in `if(requireNamespace(...))` | **Yes**, one hit: `status_message()` used `withr::with_options()`. |

The `withr` example is rewritten in base R rather than guarded. That removes the
`Suggests` use instead of hiding it, and satisfies the separate rule that an
example restores anything it changes. `withr` stays in `Suggests` for the tests.

Two things turned up while reading the package the way a reviewer would:

* `cache_dir()` defaulted to `data/cache`, a path relative to whatever directory
  R started in. CRAN policy is that a package writes outside `tempdir()` only
  where a user expects it to. It is now `tools::R_user_dir("biohttp", "cache")`.
  This is a behaviour change for anyone who had opted into the disk tier.
* A blank `BIOHTTP_CACHE_DIR` was read literally rather than falling back, so
  exporting the name with no value meant the working directory. `env_num()` and
  `env_flag()` had always treated a blank setting as one nobody made; `env_chr()`
  makes the directory read the same way.

Also: `inst/CITATION` now ships, so `citation("biohttp")` carries the Zenodo DOI
from an installed copy rather than only from a source checkout.

## Why

Submitting without this means at least one round trip on the `withr` example,
which is a known-in-advance rejection, plus a plausible second on the cache
directory.

## Checks run locally

- [x] `prek run --all-files`
- [x] `Rscript -e 'devtools::test()'` (365 pass, 0 fail, 0 skip)
- [x] `Rscript -e 'rcmdcheck::rcmdcheck(args = c("--no-manual", "--as-cran"))'`
      (0 errors, 0 warnings, 1 note: `New submission`)
- [x] `_R_CHECK_DEPENDS_ONLY_=true R CMD check` on the built tarball, examples
      and vignettes included: `Status: OK`
- [x] `urlchecker::url_check()` and `spelling::spell_check_package()`

One caveat worth recording: the depends-only run is weaker evidence than it
looks, because httr2 imports withr and that library is built recursively, so the
old example would have passed it too. The reliable check is textual, and no
`Suggests` name now appears anywhere in `R/` or `man/`.

## Scope

- [x] Stays inside the lines in `CONTRIBUTING.md`: no Shiny, no service-specific
      knowledge, no parsing beyond JSON and text, no vendor-specific retry or
      rate-limit numbers.
- [ ] **`tools` is added to `Imports`, and this is the conversation.** The
      frozen-dependency test and `CONTRIBUTING.md` are amended together rather
      than worked around. The constraint exists because every downstream package
      and app inherits the list, and `tools` ships with R, so nobody inherits
      anything new. It is declared only because `R CMD check` wants a
      declaration for anything reached with `::`, which is the same argument
      already written down for `curl`. `CONTRIBUTING.md` now states the rule as
      "anything outside base R" so the next case is decided by a rule rather
      than by this precedent.

## If it touches behaviour

- [x] A test covers it, and the test fails without the change. Two in
      `test-cache.R`: the default is `R_user_dir()` and absolute, and a blank
      `BIOHTTP_CACHE_DIR` falls back.
- [x] `NEWS.md` says what changed.
- [x] `devtools::document()` was run and `man/` is in sync.

## Review round

A review pass over this branch found that `env_chr()` had been introduced for
`BIOHTTP_CACHE_DIR` and then not applied to the three sibling readers in
`request.R`, which left the defect it exists to prevent in place at a worse
site.

`BIOHTTP_CALLER_IDENTITY` exported with no value was taken literally, so the
header went out as `User-Agent: /0.1.2` rather than `biohttp/0.1.2`. An empty
export is how a container passes through a variable an operator never filled in.
The whole suite ran that way, because `setup.R` clears those three variables by
exporting them empty, and nothing asserted on the result. There is now a test
that fails without the fix.

Two smaller things from the same pass: the `inst/CITATION` title had been split
across a `paste()` to satisfy a line limit that applies to nothing in `inst/`,
and the README status blockquote carried a line of maintainer commentary that
CRAN would have rendered on the package page.

One review finding was withdrawn after checking it. The absoluteness assertion
in the cache directory test looked redundant next to the exact-path assertion
above it, but a relative default fails it and passes everything else, since a
relative path is indistinguishable from an absolute one until something resolves
it. Both assertions stay, with a comment saying what each is for.

## Deliberately not in here

* **No CRAN badge and no `install.packages("biohttp")`.** Both point at
  `https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=biohttp`, which 404s until acceptance, and
  `README.md` ships in the tarball. Adding them now manufactures an invalid-URL
  note in the very submission they describe. They belong in a `docs:` PR after
  acceptance.
* **No `\value` in `man/STATUS_LEVELS.Rd`.** It is an exported data object
  documented with `\format`, which is the convention CRAN accepts.
* **The version bump rides along here** rather than in a separate
  `chore/version-0-1-2` PR as in #27. Happy to split it out if you would rather
  keep that pattern.

## Before submitting

`cran-comments.md` lists only the environments actually run. `check_win_devel()`
and `check_mac_release()` submit to external services, so they were left for you
to run, and the file should gain them once they come back.

title: ci: check against r-devel on windows as well as ubuntu
description:
Adds `{ os: windows-latest, r: "devel" }` to the R-CMD-check matrix.

## Why

Windows plus r-devel is the pair CRAN's own incoming check runs when a
tarball is submitted. r-lib's `examples/check-standard.yaml`, which this
matrix was copied from, puts devel on ubuntu only, so that combination was
the one thing nothing here covered.

The gap was being filled by hand with `devtools::check_win_devel()`, which
uploads a tarball to win-builder and emails the result back. That works, but
it depends on someone remembering to do it, and the result arrives somewhere
the repository cannot see. A matrix entry runs on every pull request instead.

Worth recording what this does **not** solve. The review comments CRAN raised
on a sibling package were about references in the Description field,
commented-out code in examples, and `Suggests` guards. None of those are
machine-detectable, and no amount of platform coverage would have caught
them. This closes a check-coverage gap, not a review-readiness one.

## Not required for merge, deliberately

`main`'s protection lists ten required checks by name, and the new job
reports as `R-CMD-check (windows-latest, devel)`, which is not among them. It
runs and reports without blocking.

That is the intended starting state. Windows r-devel is the least stable
square in the matrix, because CRAN's Windows r-devel binaries sometimes lag
and dependencies then build from source through Rtools. Making it required
immediately means an upstream hiccup blocks every merge, a release PR
included. Promote it once it has a track record.

## Checks

The change is one matrix entry. The workflow parses, and `prek run
--all-files` is clean.

title: release: 0.1.1
description:
Everything in 0.1.1 came out of the first real migration onto 0.1.0, which is
where a transport contract meets an app that already had its own opinions.

Closes #21
Closes #22
Closes #23

## What is in it

**#21, the one that was actually costing something.** `cache_reset()` dropped
the singleton, so a reference taken from `cache()` earlier pointed at a dead
object: writes went somewhere nothing else could see, reads came back stale, and
the only symptom was a hit rate quietly falling to zero. The reset now clears in
place when no cache setting has changed and rebuilds only when one has, which is
what test isolation needs. Neither option proposed in the issue worked, because
the rebuild is load-bearing for the disk-tier tests.

**#22.** `BIOHTTP_CACHE_MAX_N` bounds the memory tier by entry count.
`BIOHTTP_CACHE_MAX_SIZE` bounds bytes, and a long-running process answering many
small responses stays well under that while holding far more entries than
intended. Defaults to `cachem`'s own `Inf`, so nothing changes unless it is set.

**#23.** `status_message()` produces every user-facing sentence in the package,
and `options(biohttp.status_message = ...)` replaces them. The scope was wider
than the issue described: the sentences lived in two places and had already
drifted three ways for "temporarily unavailable". They share one set now.

## Wording changes a consumer may render

* `status_error()`'s default gains "Please try again."
* A 408 now reads "took too long to respond" rather than "could not retrieve".
  `classify_http()` has always called 408 a timeout, so the envelope said
  `timeout` while the sentence said something else.

## One defect found while reviewing this branch

Routing `http_error_message()` through `classify_http()` made it return `NULL`
for a 2xx, because the enum correctly calls 200 `ok`. That function's contract
is a sentence, and a 2xx genuinely reaches it: a 200 carrying an HTML error
page, or a body that will not parse. The envelope path was saved by
`status_error()`'s fallback, so it only bit a direct caller.

Every test passed either way. It turned up by diffing every status code against
0.1.0 behaviour, and is fixed in #28 with tests covering both the direct call
and the end to end path.

## Also on this branch since the last release

The hex logo and favicons, and the r-universe note in the README.

## Verification

360 tests pass. `R CMD check --as-cran` is 0 errors, 0 warnings, and the two
known notes. air clean, 0 lints, prek clean.

title: release: hex logo, r-universe, and CI on every pull request
description:
Second release since 0.1.0 was tagged. No package code changed, so the version
stays at 0.1.0. This is presentation and process.

**The hex logo.** `man/figures/logo.png` and `logo.svg` are wired into the
README and the site. pkgdown uses the SVG for the navbar and generates the
favicon set from it, which the site has never had.

The pkgdown theme needed retuning to go with it. `primary` was still `#1a6b54`,
a green chosen before the logo existed, which would have put a green navbar
beside a rust hex. It is now `#8a3a30`, taken from the logo itself.

**r-universe.** biohttp 0.1.0 is built with binaries for R 4.5.3 through 4.7.0.
The README now says so, carries the version badge, and its install instructions
are true. Verified by installing from r-universe into a clean library and making
a call, which returned an ok envelope with a parsed body. Also documents
installing from GitHub for anyone who needs an unreleased commit.

**CI on every pull request.** The workflows were restricted to pull requests
into `main` back when Actions minutes were exhausted. The repository is public
and standard runners are free, so that trade only cost safety. `secret-scan`
mattered most: a credential could reach `dev` with no server-side scan at all.

Merging this republishes the documentation site, which is where the logo and the
new theme become visible.

title: release: add the Zenodo DOI
description:

Adds the DOI badge and a "Citing biohttp" section to the README, and records

Zenodo minted two: the concept DOI (`10.5281/zenodo.21731864`), which always

description:

title: release: biohttp 0.1.0
description:
First release. Brings `main` from the initial commit up to the full package.

## What lands

- The transport: `get_json()`, `post_json()`, `get_text()`, `perform()`,
  `perform_text()`, and `req_defaults()`.
- The envelope contract. Every call returns a value and never raises on an HTTP
  or a parse failure. Seven statuses, `ok` derived so it cannot disagree.
- Per-host circuit breaking, where only a transport failure counts against a
  host.
- A success-only cache, memory by default with an opt-in disk tier.
- Batched calls, with repeated queries in a batch collapsed to one request.
- Query-string credentials via `secret_query`, attached at dispatch so the
  request object and the cache key never hold them.
- `as_legacy_envelope()`, deprecated on arrival, for migrating an app that
  returns the older four-field shape.

## Notes

Workflows now run only at this gate, so this pull request is the first CI run
for all of the above. Everything was verified locally first: 314 tests pass,
`R CMD check --as-cran` reports 0 errors and 0 warnings, 0 lints, and the
pkgdown site builds.

Two check notes are expected. CRAN incoming feasibility flags the repository
URLs as 404 because the repository is private, and there is an environmental
`NULL` check-directory note reproducible on a minimal one-function package.

Merging this publishes the documentation site to
https://www.samuelbharti.com/biohttp/ for the first time.
